headline.main: Know-How and Expertise: European Companies Hoping to Take the Global Lead in Industrial AI
headline.social: Know-How and Expertise: European Companies Hoping to Take the Global Lead in Industrial AI

intro: The U.S and China are far ahead when it comes to artificial intelligence. But industrial leaders in Europe, and especially in Germany, are hoping to find their footing with AI tools aimed specifically at making production facilities more efficient.
text:
The Audi factory in Neckarsulm is a carefully choreographed technical ballet, with 2,500 robots producing 1,000 car bodies each day – welding, soldering and gluing myriad parts together. Hardly a person is to be seen. It is modern industrial production at its finest, operating with maximum efficiency.
Almost.
There is still room for improvement.
At one point in the production line, orange robot arms weld small bolts onto the floor panel of a car body. There is a flash of light as a camera takes a picture before the car skeleton moves on to the next station.
Then, something amazing happens. In a gray cabinet next to the conveyor belt, an artificial intelligence program developed by Audi processes the images and is able to recognize where the welding robot has left behind spatter that might later create problems, such as damaging a cable. A Siemens-produced control device passes the information along to the next station, where an employee in welding goggles has 20 seconds to check the body for splatter and file it down.
Such a task would be virtually impossible without AI. With AI, however, it is simple. The control device activates spotlights which show the areas the worker must tend to. The man and his colleagues have spent months training the AI program to differentiate between potentially damaging splatter and inconsequential spots.
Soon, a robot will also take over the task of filing down the splatter, all with the help of AI. It will make Audi that much more efficient – and cost the employee his job.
Audi alone has already introduced around 100 such AI programs or is currently developing them. And the company is not alone. Across Germany, engineers, software developers and managers are striving to improve efficiency, quality control and maintenance with the help of AI, in addition to speeding up planning processes and accelerating product development.
Industrial production is entering a new era. "AI applications will revolutionize industry around the world,” says Asutosh Padhi, head of strategy at the consulting agency McKinsey in Chicago. Complex mass production, such as in the automotive industry, will achieve new levels of efficiency and quality, he says, while it will also become easier to offer customized products.
"Those who don’t join in, though, are out,” says Padhi. The next three years will be crucial, he adds. But he believes that European companies have "a huge opportunity.”
AI as an opportunity? Thus far, large language models such as those made available by OpenAI, Google and Meta have dominated, with competition coming at most from Chinese products like DeepSeek or Alibaba. Thus far, though, they have left a gap.
American technology companies use their AI models primarily to make consumers happy, replace employees at call centers with chatbots and to improve all manner of services. In short, they tend to be oriented toward the consumer. Which has opened up an opportunity for European companies, particularly those in Germany. "There is no reason why Germany shouldn’t become the global leader in industrial AI applications,” says Sabina Jeschke, a member of several supervisory boards and head of the Berlin innovation network KI Park.
Aside from China, there is likely no other country in the world that possesses such a diverse industrial landscape and so much production know-how as Germany. Automobile producers, chemical plants, pharmaceutical giants and electronic firms combine to form the backbone of the economy. Many of these companies, though, are facing tremendous pressure. Energy has become more expensive, and Donald Trump has targeted Europe with 15-percent tariffs. Increasing competition from China, European interstate bickering and bureaucratic hurdles are also doing their part to hamstring the continent’s competitiveness.
If the companies in this country of engineers were able to develop the best AI toolbox in the world, they could once again become more competitive and, in the best case, transform this toolbox into a new driver of exports. That, at least, is the hope of German industrial leaders – and it is far from illusory.
AI models are as good as the data they are fed with. In contrast to the information used to develop large language models, industrial data is not freely available on the internet. It belongs to the companies themselves, and they can use that information to train AI models and develop new applications.
Companies like Siemens, the French firm Schneider Electric or the Swiss-Swedish operation ABB want to be at the forefront of this AI revolution. All of them are global leaders in industrial automation. Siemens claims that its automated tools control machines in almost a third of all factories in the world. In the future, they are to be supported by AI.
Will Europeans be successful in using their treasure trove of data to produce AI applications and successfully market them around the world?
To do so, a mini-industrial revolution would be necessary. And to understand why, it is necessary to return to the Audi factory on the banks of the Neckar. To the Böllinger Höfe, an Audi production facility for limited series vehicles where the e-tron GT is assembled, an electric sports car with up to 925 horsepower. The factory is a cross between a manufacturing plant and a high-tech laboratory, the ideal place to try out new things.
Just like in Audi’s bigger factories, there are small control devices and computers at each station here too, regulating the production activities and processing data.
That, though, is changing. The devices and computers are slowly vanishing. In the future, production data will be sent directly to a data cloud, which Audi calls EC4P – or Edge Cloud for Protection – a data center developed by Audi with the help of Siemens and other partners where data can be centrally stored and processed.
Ultimately, all of the production stages will be controllable via the cloud. "Maintenance and software updates will be significantly faster and cheaper,” says project manager Sven Müller. Should something break, it will no longer be necessary to repair or replace dozens of computers. Software replaces hardware. Müller compares it with the switch from iPods to Spotify.
And the real innovation is the fact that all of the data in the data center can be processed by artificial intelligence and used for applications. For small tasks, such as the removal of welding spatter in the production of car bodies – or for larger processes, like the direction of entire orchestras of robots.
Starting this fall, plans call for the use of the Edge Cloud for the production of Audi’s A5 and A6 sedans, says Sebastian Reinisch, head of data analytics for Audi. Later, other factories will also receive the Edge Cloud.
Why not just control everything from the Amazon cloud in Frankfurt? "The data must be transmitted as securely and as rapidly as possible,” says Reinisch. That can be done more reliably if there is an Edge Cloud platform at each factory, he says.
Essentially, the Edge Cloud strategy is Audi’s plan for using artificial intelligence not just for isolated tasks, but on a large scale. At the company’s headquarters in Ingolstadt, Reinisch and his team have developed a matrix showing all the places where AI could be used and what must be done to prepare for that usage: data, networks, data centers, programmers.
It is an enormous effort. And one that can be undertaken almost exclusively by large companies. Within Germany’s extensive palette of mid-sized companies, by contrast, there has been relatively little movement.
Interest in generative AI (GenAI) – a label that refers to AI models that can develop new content or applications on its own from data patterns – is continuously growing, according to a study compiled by the consultants at Strategy& in Munich on behalf of the German industrial association VDMA. Its use, though, has thus far largely been limited to experimental projects, the study found.
Most mid-sized companies belonging to the VDMA complain that there is a lack of quality data and AI specialists, and that the IT infrastructure isn’t adequate. Many companies, says Bernd Jung, a partner at Strategy&, are looking "with high expectations at the possibilities” offered by GenAI to become more productive and more profitable. At the same time, they haven’t been willing to take the risk of broadly deploying artificial intelligence and developing new business models. Sometimes, he says, there is simply a lack of sufficient funds to do so.
What would happen, though, if there was a kind of off-the-shelf "foundation model” available to everyone? A model which – like the well-known foundation models GPT-4.1, Gemini and Llama – offers numerous different applications, but which is developed for the needs of industry?
It’s late May, and Peter Körte has an important presentation in the House of Communication, a trendy co-working complex in the Werksviertel business center in Munich. Wearing sneakers and a white sweater, the chief technology officer for Siemens takes the stage at the AI summit held by the company. His answer to the question as to whether Europe can take on a leading role in artificial intelligence? "Yes, we can.”
Unsurprisingly, he sees Siemens taking a leading role. "We want to build the first industrial foundation model in the world,” he says. The first applications, he promises, will be available by the end of the year.
Industrial AI, he promises, won’t just be able to work with text, spoken language and images, like existing models, but also with formulas, CAD drawings, robotic movement data, machine behavior patterns and supply chain information. This data will be translated by the model into a single language that the AI will then be able to use. But where will the huge volume of data come from that is needed to train the model?
Siemens is using data from its own factories and development laboratories. But that, alone, isn’t sufficient to prepare the voracious AI models for their complex tasks. Which is why Körte is seeking to convince Siemens customers – companies that are already buying industrial hardware and software from Siemens – to share their data. In return, they will receive cheaper access to Siemens AI applications, such as Industrial Copilot, an AI-based assistant.
It has been a slow start. According to Siemens, just 60 companies have agreed to share their data – out of more than 300,000 industrial firms in Germany. That is far too few if Germany hopes to compete with the U.S. and China.
There are discussions among European industrial leaders aimed at forming a larger European alliance, including the French AI company Mistral. But time is of the essence. American AI giants have long since identified German industry as a target. OpenAI head Sam Altman, for example, toured through Germany in the spring and announced the opening of an office in Munich.
But is the development of an industrial foundation model the right strategy? Experts like Sabine Jeschke, the head of KI Park in Berlin, have their doubts. "Instead of focusing on a single industrial foundation model, I believe an ecosystem of specialized, more flexible models would make more sense,” she says. Given the extreme speed of innovation, adaptability is decisive. Some of Siemens’ own competitors are also taking a different approach.
On a Tuesday in late June, Tanja Rückert, the chief digital officer at Bosch, takes the stage in a mint-colored jumpsuit in the Feuerbach district of Stuttgart for Tech Day. In the foyer, the Bosch is presenting AI products it has developed for the household, such as a children’s bed called Revol, which automatically weighs newborns as they sleep while also keeping tabs on their heartbeat and breathing.
Rückert’s focus, though, is on more proactive AI applications that can make decisions on their own and control processes. Such AI agents, she believes, will give industry a boost comparable to the erstwhile advances triggered by smartphones and the internet. If a machine breaks down, the agent will check if the same problem has already been experienced in a different Bosch factory, examines handbooks and scans shift logs – before then proposing a possible solution within seconds. For more complex tasks, several agents can be combined, which then communicate with each other.
Comprehensive use of such tools, says Rückert, can translate into millions in savings for individual factories. Bosch, though, doesn’t just want to use AI to save money. Rückert is hoping to make the agent system available for sale to industrial customers by the end of the year. The companies will be able to feed the system with their own data, without having to share their own data and company secrets with Bosch, in contrast to the Siemens system.
Indeed, an AI startup scene for industry has begun developing. The appliedAI Institute for Europe in Munich now lists 687 startups, of which a growing number have begun focusing on AI solutions for industrial production, logistics and development.
The Augsburg-based company plus10, for example, a spinoff of the Fraunhofer Institute for Manufacturing Engineering and Automation, has developed a continuously learning analysis software that can determine the causes of machine errors and identify possible corrective measures on a case-by-case basis, thus preventing the mass production of defective parts. Co-founder Felix Georg Müller promises at least 10 percent more error-free output – a promise that gave the company its name. Plus10’s customers include companies like Freudenberg, Boehringer Ingelheim and Continental. Its software is already active in machines producing insulin shots, a multi-billion-euro market. "We are able to finance ourselves and our growth completely through operational revenues,” says Müller.
It is an example showing that brain power is more important than capital when it comes to the successful development of AI. Companies hoping to become large and influential, however, need partners.
No matter how advanced their models and agents might be, whether its Audi, Bosch or plus10 – they are all, in some way, dependent on the Americans for the time being. Almost all of their applications, and even Siemens’ industrial foundation model, rely on available large language models from the U.S. German industrial giants usually use the data centers offered by Microsoft, Azure, Amazon and Google, with their incredibly large compute and storage capabilities. They depend on Nvidia for chips.
So does that mean that the dream of European dominance in industrial AI is just that, a dream? No, says Peter Weckesser, digital chief at the French company Schneider Electric. "The Europeans don’t have to stick their heads in the sand,” he says, adding that there are dependencies in both directions. Nvidia has most of its chips produced by the chip giant TSMC, which requires machines from ASML in Holland, which depend on technology from Germany, like lasers from Trumpf and optics from Zeiss.
Furthermore, AI programs like Meta’s Llama are being offered as open-source software, making them essentially a raw material, says Weckesser. The rise of the Chinese company DeepSeek also demonstrates, he points out, just how quickly the market develops. There are also European foundation models on offer, such as that developed by Mistral, which have tremendous potential.
Which leaves the large computing centers, where data is stored and AI models are trained. Weckesser sees three possible paths. The first involves companies continuing to rely on American clouds. The second is using their services through partners like Orange, Capgemini or Deutsche Telecom in accordance with European law to ensure that U.S. tech giants don’t have access to sensitive data.
The third possibility is for Europe to build its own data centers. "Data for critical infrastructure – such as intelligence electricity grids, such as those built by Schneider – should absolutely remain in Europe.”
That is something the European Commission wants as well. Brussels has proclaimed the ambitious, some would say misguided, goal of transforming Europe into a "leading AI continent.” Gigafactories are to be one cornerstone of that strategy, "compute and data storage hubs” for the development of "applications at hyperscale,” according to a Commission statement.
Seventy-six companies have indicated an interest in investing in such gigafactories. Several German consortiums are said to be among them, including a group including the software company SAP, Telekom and the Schwarz Group, which is building an AI research center in Heilbronn, in addition to an initiative supported by the state of Bavaria.
There is, however, plenty of skepticism within German companies. Everyone wants to be part of the project, but it is completely unclear who wants to make what contribution. Companies like Siemens see themselves as potential users of such gigafactories, or as equipment providers, while the insurance giant Allianz can envision itself as an investor. The largest question, though, remains how such a factory could be operated at a profit, such that such a huge investment might also produce a return.
"The key question is whether and how it can be ensured that such a factory is used to full capacity,” says Gerhard Kreß, lead of portfolio and digitalization at Siemens. That would require the reliable use of such a center’s computing capacities, for industrial AI applications, for example.
This fall, the EU will begin accepting concrete proposals for the construction of such gigantic data centers. Only then will crucial details begin coming into focus, such as where the electricity for the factories should come from and what role public money might play in financing.
Jeschke, the AI expert, is urging pragmatism. "A single large project can have symbolic importance,” she says, "but for the industrial use of AI, diversified, scalable data centers are often the better solution.” Such structures can be built closer to the companies, she says, which would improve efficiency, data sovereignty and the speed of innovation. The Audi solution.
The EU and its member states are providing 10 billion euros for the construction of AI factories and intend to establish a fund with an additional 20 billion. Critics from European industry, though, see the Commission as more of a hurdle – primarily because of the AI Act, which is intended to reduce the possible risks associated with artificial intelligence.
After her speech at Tech Day, Bosch executive Rückert takes a seat in a meeting room. The smell of popcorn is in the air – produced, unsurprisingly, by a machine operated with AI. Europe, she says, has a clear competitive advantage when in industrial AI. "But I fear that those who complicate the development and use of AI with overly strict regulations will not win the race.”
It sounds like she is saying: Only Europe can beat itself.
